notes.title: The GIL — What It Actually Is
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Glossary: global interpreter lock · 📘 sys.setswitchinterval · 📜 PEP 703: Making the GIL optional · 📜 PEP 684: A per-interpreter GIL · 🔬 Super Fast Python: threading guide · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: What is the GIL

⚡ TL;DR

One lock per interpreter: only the thread holding it runs Python bytecode. It's released around blocking calls and forced off every ~5 ms, so threads overlap I/O but not Python computation.

🧭 Flow: thread A runs bytecode holding the GIL ─▶ thread B waits 5 ms ─▶ B sets a drop request ─▶ A releases at its next eval-breaker check ─▶ the OS picks who runs ─▶ a blocking call (recv, sleep) releases it with no waiting at all

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does the GIL protect? Interpreter state: refcounts, allocator, built-in container internals, C extensions that assume it.
When is it released? Around blocking I/O and long C work; forcibly after another thread waits the switch interval.
Default switch interval? 5 ms (sys.getswitchinterval() → 0.005).
Does it make x += 1 atomic? No: a switch can fall between read and write.
✏️ Draw by hand: the GIL hand-off B waits 5 ms ─▶ drop request ─▶ A releases at eval breaker ─▶ OS picks; I/O releases voluntarily
Ways around it? Processes, sub-interpreters (3.12+), GIL-releasing C code, free-threaded build.

💡 The idea

Threads make a web scraper fast, so why not a CPU-heavy loop? Measured on CPython 3.12, four copies of a pure-Python loop:

def score(n=10_000_000):
    t = 0
    for i in range(n): t += i * i
    return t
# → one call 0.23 s · four sequential 0.90 s · four threads 0.87 s · four processes 0.27 s

Four threads on a ten-core machine took as long as running the calls one after another, because only one was ever executing Python. The subtler cost is latency: a thread that merely wakes from a sleep waits for the lock too, up to ~24 ms at p99 next to three CPU-bound threads (Break it measures the one-thread case).

The trade: one lock around the interpreter makes refcounting and every built-in structure safe and fast for single-threaded code, and costs parallel bytecode plus latency for any thread that must wait for the lock.

⚙️ How it works

The GIL changes hands two ways: by request when a waiting thread runs out of patience, and voluntarily when the holder blocks:

The OS, not CPython, picks the winner: there's no scheduler, no priority and no fairness guarantee. The rules around that hand-off:

Rule What actually happens
What it protects Interpreter state: every refcount, the allocator, dict/list/set internals, imports, and C extensions written assuming they hold it. One lock means the single-threaded path pays nothing extra.
Who releases voluntarily C code about to block or crunch without touching Python objects (Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS): sockets, time.sleep, file I/O, select, and NumPy, hashlib, zlib, many DB drivers. So NumPy can even run in parallel.
Where the drop request is seen At the eval breaker: function entry and backward jumps (3.12). That's where the ~5–6 ms latency comes from.
Atomicity is incidental On 3.12, c["v"] += 1 in a tight loop lost no updates across four threads even at a 1 µs interval, because no check falls between its load and store. Put a Python-level call in between (a Python __hash__, a helper) and it lost 40–55%.
Removing it The free-threaded build (3.13t/3.14t, #38) ran the same four threads in about 0.3 s, against about 0.9 s with the GIL.

💻 Code

CPU-heavy work in an async service belongs on another core:

import asyncio, os
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

_cpu_pool = ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=max(1, (os.cpu_count() or 2) // 2))   # once, at startup

def score_document(text: str) -> float:          # pure Python: holds the GIL throughout
    return sum(ord(c) for c in text) / max(len(text), 1)

async def handle(request_text: str) -> dict:
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    # ❌ score_document(request_text)              blocks the loop: every request stalls
    # ❌ await asyncio.to_thread(score_document,…) frees the loop but takes the GIL from it
    score = await loop.run_in_executor(_cpu_pool, score_document, request_text)   # ✅ other core
    return {"score": score}

to_thread is right for blocking I/O; for pure-Python computation it trades the GIL with the loop thread. The process pool pays pickling in and out, so it wins when the work is large relative to its inputs.

⚠️ Break it: a thread with nothing to compute still pays.

import threading, time, statistics
def spin(stop):
    x = 0
    while not stop.is_set(): x += 1          # pure-Python CPU work: holds the GIL
def wake_delay(n=200):
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        t = time.perf_counter(); time.sleep(0.001)
        out.append((time.perf_counter() - t - 0.001) * 1000)
    return statistics.median(out)
print(f"alone: {wake_delay():.2f} ms late")
stop = threading.Event(); threading.Thread(target=spin, args=(stop,)).start()
print(f"next to spin: {wake_delay():.2f} ms late"); stop.set()
# look for: ~5 ms or more in the second line
# naive model predicts: no change, the sleeper is asleep, not competing

On CPython 3.12.13 it printed about 0.26 ms, then about 6.5 ms; on free-threaded 3.14t, about 0.26 ms both times. Waking means running bytecode, which means reacquiring the GIL from a thread that won't let go until the switch interval forces it.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: The GIL is one lock per interpreter that a thread must hold to run Python bytecode. It protects interpreter state, above all refcounts, without per-object locks, which kept CPython and C extensions simple and single-threaded code fast. So only one thread runs Python at a time: threads help I/O, because blocking calls release the GIL, but not pure-Python CPU work. And it doesn't make your code thread-safe.

Q · Mechanism — How does the GIL change hands, and who decides which thread runs next? Two ways (the sequence diagram): voluntarily, when C code blocks or does long object-free work, and by request, when a waiter's 5 ms timeout expires and it sets a drop request that the holder sees at its next eval-breaker check. Then the OS decides who acquires it. With no scheduler, priorities or fairness in CPython, a ready thread can wait several switch intervals when it has many CPU-bound neighbours.

Q · Failure — An API's p99 latency jumped after someone added a background thread that computes embeddings in pure Python. Nothing is CPU-saturated. Diagnose. The background thread holds the GIL for up to 5 ms at a time, so request threads that are ready to run wait for it (see Break it): latency, not throughput. CPU looks fine because only one core is busy. Confirm by timing GIL waits or comparing p99 with the thread paused. Fix: move the computation to a process pool, use a library that releases the GIL (NumPy, an ONNX runtime), or a separate service.

Q · Design — Design the concurrency model for a Python service that serves HTTP, calls three external APIs per request, and runs a CPU-heavy scoring step. Classify each part. The API fan-out is I/O: asyncio (or threads) overlaps it, since waits release the GIL. The scoring step is CPU: a process pool sized to cores, or a GIL-releasing native library, or a separate scoring service if it dominates. HTTP serving: several worker processes so one stuck interpreter doesn't stall all traffic. Watch event-loop lag and p99 against CPU per process first; on free-threaded builds (3.13t+), revisit threads for the CPU step.

⚖️ Compare

Threads Processes asyncio Free-threaded threads (3.13t+)
Parallel Python bytecode no yes no yes
Overlaps I/O yes yes yes yes
Shared memory yes no (pickle, shm) yes yes
Main cost GIL contention, latency startup, pickling, RAM must never block the loop per-object locks, extension support

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "The GIL makes Python code thread-safe"
    ✅ It protects interpreter internals, not your read-modify-write sequences.
    ↳ Why: a switch can fall between the load and the store of x += 1 when Python code runs in between.
    ↳ Fix: a threading.Lock around shared mutable state (synchronization hazards).
  • 🪞 "Threads are useless in Python"
    ✅ They're excellent for I/O and GIL-releasing C code.
    ↳ Why: sockets, sleeps, file I/O and NumPy kernels release the GIL while they work.
  • ❌ "A sleeping or waiting thread doesn't feel the GIL"
    ✅ Waking up means reacquiring it.
    ↳ Symptom: a sleeper wakes several ms late next to a CPU-bound thread (see Break it).
  • 🔀 Not the same: concurrency and parallelism
    ↳ Difference: threads under the GIL give overlapping progress (concurrency), not simultaneous execution of bytecode (parallelism).
    ↳ So: I/O-bound vs CPU-bound decides the tool (concurrency vs parallelism).
  • ⚠️ Don't run pure-Python CPU work in asyncio.to_thread next to an event loop.
    ↳ Why: the loop thread then waits for the GIL, slowing every request.
    ↳ Instead: a ProcessPoolExecutor or a GIL-releasing library.
  • ⚠️ Don't lower sys.setswitchinterval to "fix" latency.
    ↳ Why: more switches mean more overhead and less throughput, and contention remains.
    ↳ Instead: move the CPU work off the interpreter that serves requests.

How the lock has changed across versions (PEPs 684, 703 and 779):

Measurements in this note are CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14t on a 10-core Mac; re-measure on your target.

🕸️ Connections

Path: concurrency vs parallelism ─▶ the GIL ─▶ threading / multiprocessing ─▶ free-threaded CPython

  • Builds on reference counting: unsynchronised refcounts are the main thing the lock protects.
  • Builds on the eval loop: the drop request is only seen at its eval-breaker checks.
  • Used by concurrent.futures: choosing a thread or process pool is choosing whether to share one GIL.
  • Contrasts with sub-interpreters: one GIL per interpreter (3.12+), so isolated interpreters run in parallel.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Ruby MRI's GVL, Node's single JS thread with a libuv pool for I/O.

notes.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Concurrent execution · 🔬 Super Fast Python: Choose the right concurrency API · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Concurrency vs parallelism

⚡ TL;DR

Concurrency overlaps waiting; parallelism executes at the same instant on different cores. I/O-bound work needs concurrency (threads, async); CPU-bound Python needs parallelism (processes, free-threading).

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Concurrency vs parallelism? Several tasks in progress, waits overlapping vs several executing at once.
What decides the tool? Whether the time goes to waiting (I/O-bound) or working (CPU-bound).
Why don't threads speed up pure-Python CPU work? The GIL: one thread runs bytecode at a time (#33).

💡 The idea

"Use threads to make it faster" is right for one kind of slow and useless for the other. Two slow jobs, measured on CPython 3.12:

import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor
def fetch(_): time.sleep(0.2)                      # I/O-bound: a 200 ms "HTTP call"
def score(n=10_000_000):                           # CPU-bound: pure computation
    t = 0
    for i in range(n): t += i * i
    return t
# sequential: 20 × fetch ≈ 4 s · 4 × score ≈ 0.90 s
with ThreadPoolExecutor(20) as ex: list(ex.map(fetch, range(20)))          # → ~0.20 s
with ThreadPoolExecutor(4) as ex:  list(ex.map(score, [10_000_000] * 4))   # → ~0.87 s
with ProcessPoolExecutor(4) as ex: list(ex.map(score, [10_000_000] * 4))   # → ~0.27 s

Threads made the waiting job twenty times faster and did nothing for the computing job; processes made the computing job about 3.5× faster. Concurrency keeps several tasks in progress so one's waiting overlaps another's. Parallelism runs several at the same instant, the only thing that helps computing.

The trade: concurrency hides waiting cheaply; parallelism multiplies computing at a higher price (processes, serialisation, memory), so the first question is always whether the time goes to waiting or to working.

⚙️ How it works

Pick by where the time goes:

Waiting releases the GIL; working holds it. A thread blocked on a socket or sleep releases the GIL, so others run during its wait: real concurrency. A thread running bytecode holds it, so a second CPU-bound thread just takes turns, same total time plus switching. C extensions that release the GIL around their inner loop are the exception.

Processes sidestep the GIL at a price. Each process has its own interpreter, so they run in parallel, paying startup, memory and pickling of arguments and results (#35). The free-threaded build (#38) makes threads parallel for CPU work: the same four score threads took about 0.3 s on 3.14t.

💻 Code

Pick the executor by workload, not by habit:

import os, sys
from concurrent.futures import Executor, ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor

def executor_for(kind: str) -> Executor:
    """kind: 'io' (network/disk/DB waits) or 'cpu' (pure-Python computation)."""
    cpus = os.process_cpu_count() if hasattr(os, "process_cpu_count") else os.cpu_count()
    if kind == "io":
        return ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=32)       # size by concurrency, not cores
    if not getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)():
        return ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=cpus)     # free-threaded: threads are parallel
    return ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=cpus)        # GIL build: only processes parallelise

os.process_cpu_count() (3.13+) respects CPU affinity, which matters in containers.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Concurrency means several tasks in progress at once, so one's waiting overlaps another's; parallelism means several executing at the same instant on different cores. In CPython, threads and asyncio give concurrency, great for I/O-bound work, but because of the GIL only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound pure Python needs processes, a GIL-releasing library, or the free-threaded build.

Q · Mechanism — Why do threads help a scraper but not a number-cruncher in CPython? The scraper's threads spend their time blocked in socket calls, and blocking calls release the GIL, so twenty threads' waits overlap and total time approaches one request. The number-cruncher's threads execute bytecode, which requires the GIL, so they take turns on one core: same total time plus switching. Measured on 3.12: 20 sleeping tasks 4 s → 0.2 s with threads; 4 CPU tasks 0.90 s → 0.87 s with threads, 0.27 s with processes.

⚖️ Compare

Threads asyncio Processes
Gives concurrency concurrency parallelism
Best for blocking I/O, GIL-releasing C many connections CPU-bound Python
Scale hundreds thousands+ about the core count
Cost GIL contention, races must never block the loop startup, pickling, RAM

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Concurrency and parallelism are the same thing"
    ✅ Concurrency overlaps waiting; parallelism executes simultaneously.
    ↳ Why it matters: the wrong one gives no speedup for your kind of slow.
  • 🪞 "More threads always means faster"
    ✅ Only when the time is spent waiting.
    ↳ Proof: four CPU-bound threads ran in 0.87 s vs 0.90 s sequential on 3.12.
  • 🔀 Not the same: I/O-bound and CPU-bound
    ↳ Difference: I/O-bound code is mostly blocked (GIL released); CPU-bound code is mostly executing (GIL held).
    ↳ Check: CPU usage near 100% of one core means CPU-bound.
  • ⚠️ Don't size I/O pools by core count.
    ↳ Why: threads mostly wait, so the limit is concurrent requests and downstream capacity, not cores.
    ↳ Instead: size by target concurrency and the dependency's limits.
  • ⚠️ Don't reach for processes for small tasks.
    ↳ Why: pickling and process overhead can exceed the work itself.
    ↳ Instead: batch work so each task is large relative to its inputs.
  • 🔖 Version: free-threaded builds 3.13t+; os.process_cpu_count() 3.13+.
    ↳ Note: timings here are CPython 3.12 and 3.14t on a 10-core Mac.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: bytecode-and-eval-loop — where bytecode runs ⬇️ Next: the-gil — why threads don't parallelise Python · concurrent-futures — the executors · async-execution-model — asyncio for many connections

notes.title: threading
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 threading · 📘 Lock objects and friends · 📘 queue · 🔬 Super Fast Python: threading guide · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Multithreading in Python

⚡ TL;DR

Threads share one heap and one GIL: blocking calls overlap, Python computation doesn't. A raw thread's errors are printed, not raised, and it can't be killed, so prefer an executor and a stop Event.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
When do threads speed things up? When work waits (sockets, files, sleep) or runs in GIL-releasing C code.
What happens to an exception in a thread? Printed by threading.excepthook; join() returns normally.
How do you stop a thread early? Cooperatively: it checks an Event; there's no kill API.
Lock vs RLock? Re-acquiring a Lock in the same thread deadlocks; RLock allows it.
Cap calls to a downstream? BoundedSemaphore(n), separate from the thread count.
Daemon thread at exit? Killed abruptly, no finally; non-daemon threads are joined.

💡 The idea

Twenty HTTP calls in a loop take twenty round trips. Put each on a thread and the waits overlap, about one round trip in total. But three things that were "just true" stop being true:

import threading
results = []
def work(n):
    if n == 3:
        raise ValueError(f"bad input {n}")
    results.append(n * n)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work, args=(n,)) for n in range(6)]
for t in threads: t.start()
for t in threads: t.join()
print(sorted(results))     # → traceback for n=3 printed, then [0, 1, 4, 16, 25]

Errors don't propagate: the ValueError was printed to stderr and join() returned normally, so a result went silently missing. State is shared: every thread sees the same results. And exit waits for non-daemon threads while daemon ones are killed mid-operation.

The trade: blocking calls overlap with almost no code change, and you take on shared state, silent errors and lifecycle you manage by hand.

⚙️ How it works

A worker releases the GIL around a blocking call, so the main thread keeps running:

Every Thread is an OS thread. The OS schedules it and the GIL decides which runnable thread executes bytecode (#33). Creation is cheap, about 36 µs to create, start and join on CPython 3.12 here, but each thread has its own stack, so thousands cost real memory.

The primitives. Lock is mutual exclusion; RLock can be re-acquired by its holder; Event is a one-bit flag, the standard shutdown signal; Condition waits for a predicate on shared state; Semaphore/BoundedSemaphore allow at most N holders; threading.local() gives per-thread attributes. queue.Queue covers most producer/consumer needs without touching them directly.

Exceptions go to threading.excepthook. An uncaught exception ends the thread and is printed by the hook (3.8+), never raised in the joiner. concurrent.futures instead stores it on the future and result() re-raises it (#36).

Daemons die at exit; threads can't be killed. The interpreter joins non-daemon threads before exiting and stops daemon threads abruptly, with no finally: a process with a daemon in a 10-second sleep exited in 0.34 s here. There's no API to kill a thread, so long-running workers must check a flag.

💻 Code

A bounded, observable fan-out with cooperative cancellation:

import logging, threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
_downstream = threading.BoundedSemaphore(8)   # at most 8 in-flight calls, whatever the thread count
_local = threading.local()                    # one HTTP session per thread
stop = threading.Event()                      # set from a signal handler to stop early

def fetch_one(url):
    if stop.is_set():
        return url, None                      # threads can't be killed: they must check
    if not hasattr(_local, "s"):
        _local.s = make_http_session()
    with _downstream:
        return url, _local.s.get(url, timeout=5).status_code

def fetch_all(urls):
    ok, failed = {}, {}
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=32, thread_name_prefix="fetch") as pool:
        futures = {pool.submit(fetch_one, u): u for u in urls}
        for fut in as_completed(futures):
            try:
                url, status = fut.result()    # the worker's exception is re-raised HERE
                ok[url] = status
            except Exception as exc:
                failed[futures[fut]] = repr(exc)
                log.warning("fetch failed: %s", exc)
    return ok, failed

The executor makes errors visible, the semaphore caps load on the downstream independently of thread count, and threading.local avoids sharing clients that aren't thread-safe.

⚠️ Break it: an unlocked counter with Python code between read and write.

import threading
class Hit:
    n = 0
def bump(times):
    for _ in range(times):
        v = Hit.n
        _ = len(str(v))                     # a little Python work between read and write
        Hit.n = v + 1
ts = [threading.Thread(target=bump, args=(100_000,)) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print(Hit.n)
# look for: well under 400000
# naive model predicts: 400000, "the GIL serialises threads"

On CPython 3.12.13 it prints well under 400,000 (the exact number varies per run). The GIL switched threads between the read and the write, so updates were lost; a Lock around the three lines fixes it (#37).

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: A threading.Thread is a real OS thread sharing the process's heap and its GIL. Threads are the simplest way to overlap blocking I/O in synchronous code, because blocking calls release the GIL; they don't parallelise pure-Python computation. The costs: shared state needs locks, an exception in a thread is printed rather than raised, and you can't kill a thread. So I use an executor for results and errors, and an Event for shutdown.

Q · Mechanism — What happens when a thread raises, and how do you make failures visible? The exception unwinds the thread's stack and goes to threading.excepthook, which prints it to stderr; the thread ends, and join() in the caller returns normally with no error. So raw threads lose failures in services whose stderr isn't watched. Options: replace threading.excepthook to log and count, or wrap the target in a try/except that records errors, or better, use ThreadPoolExecutor, where the exception is stored on the future and re-raised by result() in the caller.

Q · Failure — A batch job using threads reports success but some output rows are missing, and a counter is occasionally low. Diagnose. Two thread bugs. Missing rows: a worker raised, the exception was printed and dropped, and join() succeeded (see the idea). Low counter: an unlocked read-modify-write lost updates when the GIL switched between read and write (see Break it). Tests passed because they were small and errors only went to stderr. Fix: ThreadPoolExecutor with result() per future and a failure count that fails the job, plus a Lock around shared updates or a single-writer queue.

Q · Design — A sync Django service calls three slow downstream APIs per request. How would you add threads safely? The binding constraints are downstream capacity and request latency. A process-wide ThreadPoolExecutor created at startup (not per request), sized by target concurrency, with a BoundedSemaphore per downstream so bursts can't overload them, timeouts on every call, threading.local or thread-safe clients, and result(timeout=…) per future so a stuck call can't hang the request. Watch per-downstream in-flight counts and p99 first; if concurrency must reach thousands, move the fan-out to async.

⚖️ Compare

Lock RLock Semaphore(n) Event queue.Queue
Purpose mutual exclusion re-entrant exclusion cap concurrent holders one-bit signal producer/consumer channel
Re-acquire by holder deadlocks allowed counts down — —
Typical use guard shared state recursive code rate of downstream calls shutdown hand work between threads

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "join() re-raises a thread's exception"
    ✅ It only waits; the exception was printed and dropped.
    ↳ Symptom: a job "succeeds" with results missing.
    ↳ Fix: ThreadPoolExecutor and future.result().
  • 🪞 "The GIL makes my shared counter safe"
    ✅ The GIL can switch between your read and your write.
    ↳ Proof: four threads ended well under 400,000 (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: a Lock, or one writer fed by a queue.Queue.
  • ❌ "I can stop a stuck thread from outside"
    ✅ Python has no API to kill a thread.
    ↳ So: every long-running worker must check an Event, and every blocking call needs a timeout.
  • 🔀 Not the same: threads and parallelism
    ↳ Difference: threads give concurrency for waiting; on a GIL build they don't run Python in parallel.
    ↳ So: CPU-bound pure Python needs processes or the free-threaded build.
  • ⚠️ Don't mark a thread daemon to make shutdown "easy" when it writes data.
    ↳ Why: daemons are killed mid-operation, with no finally, at exit.
    ↳ Instead: a non-daemon thread that checks a stop Event and flushes.
  • ⚠️ Don't share HTTP sessions or DB connections across threads unless documented safe.
    ↳ Why: many clients keep per-connection state that interleaves badly.
    ↳ Instead: threading.local() or a thread-safe pool.
  • 🔖 Version: threading.excepthook 3.8+; on free-threaded 3.13t+ threads run Python in parallel, so races appear more often.
    ↳ Note: thread start cost and timings here are CPython 3.12.13 on macOS.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: the-gil — why threads overlap waits but not work · concurrency-vs-parallelism — choosing the tool ⬇️ Next: concurrent-futures — futures carry results and errors · synchronization-hazards — locks, deadlocks, queues · bridging-sync-async — threads from async code

notes.title: multiprocessing
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Contexts and start methods · 📘 pickle · 📘 multiprocessing.shared_memory · 🔬 Super Fast Python: multiprocessing guide · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: Multiprocessing in Python

⚡ TL;DR

Each process has its own interpreter and GIL, so Python runs in parallel, and nothing is shared by default. Everything that crosses (arguments, results, exceptions) is pickled, so send small inputs and load big state once per worker.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Why do processes parallelise CPU work? One interpreter and GIL each, on different cores.
What crosses the boundary, and how? Arguments, results, exceptions, pickled; functions travel by importable name.
spawn vs fork vs forkserver? Fresh interpreter / copy of the parent / fork from a clean helper.
Default start method? spawn on macOS and Windows; forkserver on other POSIX from 3.14.
Why is if __name__ == "__main__": required? spawn and forkserver re-import the main module in each child.
The fork-with-threads trap? Locks held by other threads are copied locked with no thread to release them.

💡 The idea

Threads can't run pure-Python computation in parallel, so send it to another process. On CPython 3.12, four copies of a CPU-bound loop took 0.90 s sequentially, 0.87 s on threads and 0.27 s on four processes. But look at what one call costs and what fails:

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
def total(d): return sum(d)
data = list(range(5_000_000))                  # total(data) inline: ~0.011 s
with ProcessPoolExecutor(1) as ex:
    ex.submit(total, data).result()            # → ~0.11 s in a worker: 10× slower
    ex.submit(lambda x: x * 2, 21).result()    # → PicklingError: Can't pickle <function <lambda>…>

The extra time is data pickled into ~25 MB of bytes (CPython 3.12), piped to the child, unpickled into a new list, and the result pickled back. Nothing is shared: the child has its own copy. And pickle sends functions by name, so a lambda or nested function can't make the trip.

The trade: real CPU parallelism by giving each worker its own interpreter and GIL, paid in startup time, memory per process, and pickling everything that crosses.

⚙️ How it works

The start method decides what a child begins with; every call then crosses as pickle:

Start methods. spawn starts a fresh interpreter and re-imports your main module: safest, slowest, and why the __main__ guard is mandatory. fork copies the parent's address space instantly, globals and all, but also the state of every lock, without the threads holding them: a lock held at fork time stays locked forever, the classic child hanging at 0% CPU. forkserver forks from a clean helper, most of fork's speed without a multi-threaded parent's state.

The defaults moved. spawn is the default on macOS (since 3.8) and Windows. From 3.12, forking a multi-threaded process warns; from 3.14 fork is no longer the default anywhere, and Linux defaults to forkserver. Here on macOS, starting and stopping a Pool(4) took ~30 ms with spawn, ~4 ms with fork, ~32 ms with forkserver; real imports make spawn pay again in every child.

Everything crosses as pickle. Arguments, results and exceptions are pickled; functions and classes by reference (module.qualname), so they must be top-level. Large arguments cost their full serialisation per call; chunksize on map batches small tasks into fewer round trips.

Sharing, when you must. shared_memory.SharedMemory gives processes one block of raw bytes, ideal for a NumPy array with no pickling. Value/Array are small locked shared values. Manager proxies are convenient and slow (every access is a round trip). Read-only state loaded before fork is shared for free until something writes, including refcount and GC-header writes (#28, #29).

💻 Code

CPU-heavy batch scoring, with expensive state loaded once per worker:

import multiprocessing as mp
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

_model = None                                     # per-worker global

def _init_worker(model_path):
    global _model
    _model = load_model(model_path)               # once per PROCESS, not per task

def score_batch(rows):                            # top-level: pickle sends it by name
    return [_model.score(r) for r in rows]

def score_all(rows, model_path, workers=8, size=1_000):
    ctx = mp.get_context("spawn")                 # same behaviour on macOS, Linux, 3.14+
    batches = (rows[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(rows), size))   # few big tasks
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers, mp_context=ctx,
                             initializer=_init_worker, initargs=(model_path,)) as pool:
        return [s for scores in pool.map(score_batch, batches) for s in scores]

if __name__ == "__main__":                        # required: children re-import this module
    print(len(score_all(load_rows(), "model.bin")))

Batching amortises per-task pickling and IPC, which dominates when tasks are small.

⚠️ Break it: mutate a "shared" module global.

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
seen = []
def record(x):
    seen.append(x)                     # appends to the CHILD's copy
    return len(seen)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(2) as ex:
        print("child-side:", list(ex.map(record, range(6))))
    print("parent sees:", seen)
# look for: children report growing lengths, parent's list is EMPTY
# naive model predicts: parent sees [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], as with threads

On CPython 3.12.13 the children report growing lengths (how they split depends on which worker takes each task) and the parent prints []. Each worker has its own globals; only return values come back.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: multiprocessing runs work in separate processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL, so pure-Python CPU work really runs in parallel. Nothing is shared by default: arguments, results and exceptions are pickled across pipes, and functions travel by name, so they must be top-level. The start method matters: spawn re-imports your module, fork copies the parent including its lock state, and since 3.14 fork isn't the default anywhere.

Q · Mechanism — Compare spawn, fork and forkserver, and explain the fork-with-threads hazard. spawn starts a fresh interpreter that re-imports the main module: no inherited state, slow startup, requires the __main__ guard. fork duplicates the parent's memory copy-on-write: instant, children inherit loaded globals, but only the forking thread is copied, so any lock another thread held (logging, an allocator, a client's connection pool) stays locked in the child and the first use deadlocks. forkserver forks from a clean single-threaded helper. Hence 3.12's warning and 3.14's change of default.

Q · Failure — A multiprocessing job is slower than the single-process version, and on Linux children sometimes hang at 0% CPU. Diagnose both. Slower: tasks are small relative to what they pickle, so serialisation and IPC dominate, for instance sending a big list or model per call. Fix with an initializer that loads state once per worker and batches with chunksize. The hang: fork from a parent with threads (a metrics exporter, a DB pool) copied a held lock (see How it works). Fix: spawn or forkserver, or fork before starting threads.

Q · Design — Nightly job: score 50 million rows with a pure-Python model on a 32-core machine. Design it. The binding constraint is what crosses the boundary. Partition rows by file or offset range so each worker reads its own input instead of receiving pickled rows; load the model in an initializer, or memory-map it so workers share pages; return small aggregates or write outputs per worker; size the pool to physical cores. Use spawn or forkserver explicitly, checkpoint per partition for retries, and watch per-worker throughput and RSS first. If the model is NumPy-heavy, threads may do instead.

⚖️ Compare

spawn fork forkserver
Child starts with re-imported modules only full copy of parent memory copy of a clean helper
Startup (Pool(4), tiny script) ~30 ms ~4 ms ~32 ms
Thread-safety hazard none inherited held locks none
Default macOS, Windows none from 3.14 other POSIX from 3.14

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "Worker processes share my module globals"
    ✅ Each has its own copy; only return values come back.
    ↳ Symptom: results dict empty in the parent (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: return results instead of mutating shared state.
  • 🪞 "Processes always make CPU work faster"
    ✅ Only when the work is large relative to what crosses the boundary.
    ↳ Proof: one call with a big list ran ~10× slower in a worker than inline.
    ↳ Fix: load state once per worker, batch tasks.
  • ❌ "Any function can be sent to a worker"
    ✅ Pickle sends functions by importable name.
    ↳ So: lambdas and nested functions raise PicklingError; define tasks at module top level.
  • 🔀 Not the same: fork and spawn
    ↳ Difference: fork copies the parent, including held locks; spawn starts fresh and re-imports your module.
    ↳ So: code that works on Linux (old fork default) can break on macOS or on 3.14.
  • ⚠️ Don't fork a process that already has threads.
    ↳ Why: a lock held by another thread is copied locked forever, and the child hangs at 0% CPU.
    ↳ Instead: spawn/forkserver, or fork before starting threads.
  • ⚠️ Don't use a Manager dict for hot shared state.
    ↳ Why: every access is a round trip to the manager process.
    ↳ Instead: return results, or shared_memory for large arrays.
  • 🔖 Version: spawn default on macOS since 3.8; fork-with-threads warning 3.12; forkserver default on Linux from 3.14.
    ↳ Note: startup timings here are macOS, tiny scripts; real imports raise them.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: the-gil — why threads can't parallelise Python · reference-counting — why fork's sharing erodes ⬇️ Next: concurrent-futures — the pool API · import-system — what spawn re-imports · asgi-wsgi-worker-model — pre-fork servers

notes.title: concurrent.futures
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 concurrent.futures · 📜 PEP 3148: futures · 🔬 Super Fast Python: ThreadPoolExecutor guide · 📖 GeeksforGeeks: ThreadPoolExecutor

⚡ TL;DR

An executor is a bounded pool; submit returns a Future that carries the result or the exception home. map yields in input order, as_completed in finishing order, wait gives deadlines; never block on the pool you're running in.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What does fut.result() do with a worker's error? Re-raises it in the caller, with the original traceback.
When does cancel() work? Only while the job is still queued; running jobs return False.
map vs as_completed? Input order (slow early item blocks the rest) vs completion order.
Default ThreadPoolExecutor size? min(32, cpu + 4): 14 on a 10-core machine.
The self-deadlock? A job waiting on another job in the same, full pool.
Deadline over a whole fan-out? wait(futures, timeout=…) → (done, not_done).

💡 The idea

Raw threads lose exceptions, have no timeout, and grow one thread per task. Hand the same work to an executor:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as ex:
    futures = {ex.submit(fetch, u): u for u in urls}
    for fut in as_completed(futures):
        try:
            print(futures[fut], fut.result())     # the worker's exception is re-raised HERE
        except Exception as e:
            print(futures[fut], "failed:", e)

The thread count is fixed at 16 however many URLs there are. Each submit returns a Future, and result() returns the value or re-raises the worker's exception in your thread. Futures combine: as_completed, wait with a timeout, cancel() for jobs not yet started. Swap in ProcessPoolExecutor and the same code runs on processes (#35); InterpreterPoolExecutor (3.14) runs it on sub-interpreters (#39).

The trade: a bounded pool and futures that carry results and errors home, in exchange for direct control over individual threads, which you rarely wanted.

⚙️ How it works

A future is a small state machine with one result slot:

A future is a state machine plus a slot. PENDING → RUNNING → FINISHED (or CANCELLED), holding a result or an exception. result(timeout) blocks until FINISHED, then returns or raises the stored exception. On 3.12, cancelling a running future returned False and a queued one True. Exceptions inside an add_done_callback are logged and ignored.

Workers pull from one queue. ThreadPoolExecutor starts threads lazily up to max_workers (default min(32, cpu + 4)). ProcessPoolExecutor pickles each call and result across processes and defaults to one worker per CPU.

Three collection styles. map yields in input order, so a slow first item holds back the rest, and an exception is raised when iteration reaches it, ending that loop. as_completed yields in finishing order. wait(fs, timeout, return_when) returns (done, not_done), the tool for deadlines and first-wins. With jobs of 0.3, 0.1 and 0.2 s: as_completed gave [0.1, 0.2, 0.3], map gave [0.3, 0.1, 0.2].

Shutdown. Leaving with calls shutdown(wait=True), waiting for every job. shutdown(cancel_futures=True) (3.9+) cancels queued jobs; the running ones still finish.

💻 Code

Request-time fan-out with a deadline and partial results:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, wait

POOL = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=32, thread_name_prefix="fanout")   # shared, created once

def fan_out(calls, budget_s=0.8):
    futures = {POOL.submit(fn): name for name, fn in calls.items()}
    done, pending = wait(futures, timeout=budget_s)        # never wait past the budget
    out = {}
    for fut in done:
        exc = fut.exception()                              # returns the error, doesn't raise
        out[futures[fut]] = {"ok": exc is None, "value": None if exc else fut.result(),
                             "error": repr(exc) if exc else None}
    for fut in pending:
        fut.cancel()                                       # only stops ones not yet started
        out[futures[fut]] = {"ok": False, "value": None, "error": "timeout"}
    return out

cancel() can't stop a running call, so each downstream call also needs its own timeout; and a per-request executor would pay thread startup on every call and let bursts create unbounded threads.

⚠️ Break it: wait on the same pool from inside it.

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, TimeoutError
import time
pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2)
def child(): time.sleep(0.01); return "child done"
def parent(): return pool.submit(child).result(timeout=1)   # waits on the SAME pool
futures = [pool.submit(parent) for _ in range(2)]            # both workers are parents
for f in futures:
    try: print(f.result())
    except TimeoutError: print("parent timed out: child never got a worker")
pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)
# look for: both parents time out, though each child needs 10 ms
# naive model predicts: "child done" twice

On CPython 3.12.13 both parents time out; without the timeout it hangs forever. Every worker was waiting for work that no worker was free to run.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: concurrent.futures gives one API over thread and process pools. submit queues work and returns a Future; result() returns the value or re-raises the worker's exception in the caller. I collect with as_completed for completion order, wait with a timeout for deadlines, and map only when input order matters. Thread pools suit I/O, process pools CPU-bound Python, and the pool is created once, not per request.

Q · Mechanism — What's the difference between map, as_completed and wait, and what does cancel() really do? map yields results in input order, so one slow early item delays every result behind it, and the first exception ends the iteration. as_completed yields futures as they finish, so each is handled as soon as it's ready. wait(timeout, return_when) returns done and pending sets, for deadlines or first-wins. cancel() only succeeds while a job is queued; once running, it returns False and the work continues, so real cancellation needs per-call timeouts or cooperative flags.

Q · Failure — A service using a shared thread pool works in staging and hangs under production load. Diagnose. Classic self-deadlock: a task submits sub-tasks to the same pool and blocks on their results. At low load there are free workers; at full load every worker is a parent waiting on queued children (see Break it). Thread dumps show all pool threads in result(). Fix: a separate pool for inner work, restructure so parents don't block (callbacks), or move the fan-out to asyncio, where awaiting doesn't hold a worker.

Q · Design — An aggregation endpoint calls 12 downstream services with an 800 ms budget. Design the concurrency. The binding constraint is the latency budget across all calls. A module-level thread pool sized for peak concurrent calls, wait(timeout=budget) over the whole fan-out, per-call client timeouts below the budget so stragglers release workers, partial results with per-service status, and a semaphore per downstream so one slow service can't consume the pool. At thousands of requests per second, asyncio with asyncio.timeout scales better. Watch pool queue depth and per-downstream p99 first.

⚖️ Compare

ex.map as_completed wait(timeout)
Order input order completion order sets: done / not done
Slow item effect blocks later results none lands in not_done
Exceptions raised when reached, ends the loop per future per future
Use for ordered results, simple batches process as ready deadlines, first-wins

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "cancel() stops a running task"
    ✅ It only stops tasks still queued.
    ↳ Why: threads can't be interrupted; a running future's cancel() returns False.
    ↳ Fix: per-call timeouts or a cooperative stop flag.
  • 🪞 "ex.map returns results as they finish"
    ✅ It yields in input order.
    ↳ Symptom: one slow first item delays every result; one exception ends the loop.
    ↳ Instead: as_completed when order doesn't matter.
  • ❌ "Creating an executor per request is fine"
    ✅ Each one starts its own threads.
    ↳ Symptom: thread startup on every request and unbounded threads under bursts.
    ↳ Fix: one shared, module-level pool.
  • 🔀 Not the same: thread and process pools
    ↳ Difference: threads share memory and are GIL-bound; processes pickle inputs and outputs and run in parallel.
    ↳ So: same API, different costs: pick by I/O-bound vs CPU-bound.
  • ⚠️ Don't block on a future from a task running in the same pool.
    ↳ Why: when every worker waits, nothing runs the work they wait on (see Break it).
    ↳ Instead: a separate pool, callbacks, or asyncio.
  • ⚠️ Don't ignore futures you submitted.
    ↳ Why: an exception stays stored on the future and is never seen unless you call result() or exception().
    ↳ Instead: collect every future, or add a done-callback that logs failures.
  • 🔖 Version: cancel_futures 3.9+; default thread count min(32, cpu + 4) since 3.8; InterpreterPoolExecutor 3.14.
    ↳ Note: measurements here are CPython 3.12.13.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: threading — what the thread pool manages · multiprocessing — what the process pool pays ⬇️ Next: synchronization-hazards — shared state between workers · tasks-gather-cancellation — the asyncio version of futures · sub-interpreters — InterpreterPoolExecutor

notes.title: Synchronization & Hazards
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 Lock objects and friends · 📘 queue · 📘 Python support for free threading · 📖 Super Fast Python: threading guide

⚡ TL;DR

Any invariant spanning more than one step needs a lock held for all of it; += is never atomic. Avoid deadlocks with one global lock order, and avoid most locks by passing ownership through queue.Queue.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Is x += 1 on shared state atomic? No: load, add, store; a switch between them loses updates.
How do you prevent lock-ordering deadlocks? Every path takes locks in one global order.
Why prefer queue.Queue? It passes ownership between threads, with blocking and backpressure built in.

💡 The idea

In single-threaded code, stats["hits"] += 1 is one indivisible step. Run it from four threads and change only what happens between the read and the write:

stats = {"hits": 0}
def bump(x): return x + 1
def record_hit():
    stats["hits"] = bump(stats["hits"])      # a function call between read and write
# 4 threads × 100,000 calls   → 400,000 of 400,000 (CPython 3.12): looks fine
# 4 threads × 1,000,000 calls → ~2.3–2.6 million of 4 million: ~40% lost

With 100,000 calls each thread finished inside one 5 ms switch interval, so the threads never actually overlapped, which is exactly how small tests hide races. At a million calls they overlap and ~40% of updates vanish. A tight stats["hits"] += 1 loop on 3.12 came out right even then, because no GIL switch point falls between its load and store (#33); the function call adds one. On free-threaded 3.14t even the tight loop lost about 70% of 800,000. It was never atomic: two threads read the same value and both write the same result.

The trade: threads buy concurrency by letting other code run between any two of your steps, so every multi-step invariant needs a lock, whether or not your tests have caught it yet.

⚙️ How it works

Decide whether to share at all, then how to lock:

Races. Any read-modify-write on shared state (+=, check-then-set, "if not in cache, compute and store") races unless a lock covers all of it. Single operations on built-ins are protected internally (list.append, d[k] = v won't corrupt the container, on GIL or free-threaded builds), but a sequence of them is never atomic.

Deadlocks. Thread 1 holds A and waits for B while thread 2 holds B and waits for A; Python threads can't be killed, so both hang. Measured with acquire(timeout=0.5), both timed out. One global acquisition order makes it impossible. A plain Lock also deadlocks against itself if one thread acquires it twice; that's what RLock is for.

queue.Queue is the safe channel. A deque behind a lock and two conditions, with blocking put/get and maxsize for backpressure: a full bounded queue blocks put and raises queue.Full on timeout. Passing ownership through it removes most of the need for locks.

💻 Code

Ordered locking for the unavoidable two-lock case, and a queue so producers and consumers never share state:

import queue, threading

class Account:
    def __init__(self, acct_id, balance):
        self.id, self.balance, self.lock = acct_id, balance, threading.Lock()

def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    first, second = sorted((src, dst), key=lambda a: a.id)   # ONE global order, by id
    with first.lock, second.lock:                            # no A→B vs B→A cycle possible
        if src.balance < amount:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")           # check and act under the same locks
        src.balance -= amount
        dst.balance += amount

work = queue.Queue(maxsize=1000)       # bounded: producers block = backpressure
STOP = object()                        # one sentinel per consumer

def consumer(handle):
    while (item := work.get()) is not STOP:                  # ownership passes with the item
        try:
            handle(item)
        finally:
            work.task_done()
    work.task_done()

The balance check and the update happen under the same locks, so no other thread can move money in between.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: Threads let other code run between any two of your steps, so read-modify-write on shared state, like += or check-then-set, races unless a lock covers the whole sequence. The GIL often hides it, until a refactor adds a function call or you run free-threaded. Deadlocks come from taking two locks in different orders, so I enforce one global order, and where I can, I avoid sharing entirely by passing work through a queue.Queue.

Q · Mechanism — Why does counter += 1 sometimes lose updates and sometimes not, on the same CPython? It compiles to load, add, store. On a GIL build, threads switch only at eval-breaker points, and a tight loop happens to have none between the load and the store, so it often works. Insert a Python call (a helper, a property, a __hash__) and a switch point appears: two threads load the same value, both store value + 1, one increment vanishes. Free-threaded builds run threads simultaneously, so it loses updates even in the tight loop. The fix is the same everywhere: a lock or a single owner.

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "x += 1 is atomic in Python"
    ✅ It's load, add, store: three steps.
    ↳ Symptom: lost updates appear after a harmless refactor or on a free-threaded build.
    ↳ Fix: a Lock around the whole sequence.
  • 🪞 "My tests pass, so the shared counter is fine"
    ✅ The GIL hides races in tight loops.
    ↳ Proof: adding one function call lost ~40% of updates on 3.12; free-threaded lost them without it.
  • ❌ "Built-in containers are thread-safe, so my code is"
    ✅ Single operations are; sequences aren't.
    ↳ Example: if k not in d: d[k] = compute() lets two threads compute and overwrite.
  • 🔀 Not the same: data race and deadlock
    ↳ Difference: a race is too little locking (wrong results); a deadlock is locks taken in conflicting order (no progress).
    ↳ So: the fixes differ: cover the invariant vs fix the order.
  • ⚠️ Don't take two locks without a global order.
    ↳ Why: two paths taking them in opposite order hang forever, and threads can't be killed.
    ↳ Instead: sort locks by a stable key, or redesign to need one.
  • ⚠️ Don't call unknown code (callbacks, logging handlers) while holding a lock.
    ↳ Why: it may take other locks or call back into you, creating an ordering you can't see.
    ↳ Instead: copy what you need under the lock, call outside it.
  • 🔖 Version: free-threaded builds (3.13t+) expose races the GIL hid.
    ↳ Note: counts here are CPython 3.12.13 and 3.14t; exact loss varies per run.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: threading — the primitives · the-gil — why races hide ⬇️ Next: no-gil-free-threaded-cpython — where races stop hiding · async-primitives-patterns — the asyncio equivalents

notes.title: No-GIL / Free-Threaded CPython
notes.html:
📚 References

📜 PEP 703: Making the GIL optional · 📜 PEP 779: Supported status for free-threaded Python · 📘 HOWTO: Python support for free threading · 📘 HOWTO: C API extension support · 🔧 py-free-threading: ecosystem readiness

⚡ TL;DR

The free-threaded build (python3.13t, 3.14t) has no GIL: threads run Python in parallel over one shared heap. It costs some single-thread speed, ~15–20% memory and extension porting, and the GIL's accidental thread safety is gone.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
Status in 3.13 vs 3.14? 3.13: experimental. 3.14: officially supported but optional (PEP 779).
How are refcounts cheap without a GIL? Biased refcounting: owner thread plain, other threads atomic.
What protects dict/list internals? Per-object locks, with lock-free fast paths for common reads.
What re-enables the GIL? Importing a C extension that doesn't declare Py_mod_gil support.
How do you check? sys._is_gil_enabled(); force with PYTHON_GIL=0/1 or -X gil=0/1.
Single-thread overhead? ~1% (macOS arm64) to ~8% (x86-64 Linux) on pyperformance, per the HOWTO.

💡 The idea

Run the identical program on both builds (a 10-core Mac):

                         3.14.6 (GIL)    3.14.6t (free-threaded)
sys._is_gil_enabled()    True            False
4 × score, sequential    0.91 s          0.83 s
4 × score, 4 threads     0.91 s          0.22–0.30 s   ← parallel
4 × score, 4 processes   0.25 s          0.22 s

Threads now run on four cores at once with no code change. And the GIL's accidental protection is gone: four threads doing 200,000 c["v"] += 1 each gave 800,000 on 3.12 and about 225,000 on 3.14t. The code was always wrong (#37); the GIL was hiding it.

The trade: real thread parallelism over one shared heap, paid with some single-threaded speed, more memory, C-extension compatibility work, and the end of hidden races.

⚙️ How it works

Removing the GIL meant replacing each job it did:

Biased reference counting (PEP 703). Atomic updates on every refcount change would crush single-thread speed. Each object records its owning thread, which updates a local count with ordinary instructions; other threads update a separate shared count atomically. Heavily shared objects (interned strings, code objects, module functions) are immortal or use deferred counting.

Per-object locks for containers. dict, list and set take a small lock per operation, with optimistic lock-free reads. Single operations behave like the GIL build (append, d[k] = v won't corrupt), but compound operations aren't atomic, and iterating while another thread mutates can show duplicated or missing items. Contention is real: four threads appending to one list were several times slower on 3.14t than with a list each (0.026 s vs 0.007 s in one run; 0.064 vs 0.014 in another).

Memory, GC and extensions. The build uses mimalloc instead of pymalloc (#31) and a stop-the-world, non-generational collector; some memory is reclaimed only after all threads pass a safe point, and PEP 779 reports ~15–20% more memory on pyperformance. An extension must declare support via the Py_mod_gil slot, or importing it re-enables the GIL for the whole process with a warning.

💻 Code

Correct on both builds, and visible about which one it's on:

import os, sys, threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

FREE_THREADED = not getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", lambda: True)()   # False if an extension re-enabled it
MODEL = load_model_once()                     # ONE copy shared by every thread
_stats_lock = threading.Lock()
_stats = {"requests": 0, "errors": 0}

def handle(features):
    try:
        return MODEL.predict(features)        # safe only if predict() never mutates the model
    except Exception:
        with _stats_lock:
            _stats["errors"] += 1             # read-modify-write: locked on every build
        raise
    finally:
        with _stats_lock:
            _stats["requests"] += 1

workers = (os.process_cpu_count() or 4) if FREE_THREADED else 4    # CPU-sized only if parallel
POOL = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers)
log_startup(f"free_threaded={FREE_THREADED} workers={workers}")    # surfaces a silent GIL re-enable

Many ML libraries cache internally during predict; a cache written from several threads is a race.

⚠️ Break it: run this with python3.14 and python3.14t.

import sys, threading
counts = {"n": 0}
def work():
    for _ in range(200_000):
        counts["n"] += 1               # unsynchronised read-modify-write
ts = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print(f"GIL: {sys._is_gil_enabled()}  count: {counts['n']:,} of 800,000")
# look for: 800,000 with the GIL; far fewer without
# naive model predicts: 800,000 on both, "dict operations are thread-safe"

On 3.14.6 it printed GIL: True count: 800,000; on 3.14.6t, GIL: False and about 225,000–250,000 (it varies per run). The dict stayed intact on both; the program's invariant didn't. This is the first test to run before moving threaded code to free-threading.

🗣️ Interview

30-second answer: The free-threaded build, PEP 703, experimental in 3.13 and officially supported but optional in 3.14, removes the GIL, so threads run Python bytecode in parallel over one shared heap. It replaces what the GIL did with biased refcounting, per-object locks on containers, mimalloc, and an opt-in for C extensions. Costs: a few percent single-thread overhead, more memory, extensions to port, and races the GIL used to hide now show up.

Q · Mechanism — Why couldn't CPython just delete the GIL, and what did PEP 703 build instead? The GIL did four jobs. Refcounts change on almost every operation; naive atomics would slow everything, so biased refcounting lets the owning thread use plain updates and others atomic ones, with immortal and deferred counting for hot shared objects. Container internals assumed one writer, so they got per-object locks with lock-free reads. The allocator and GC assumed single-threaded access, so mimalloc and a stop-the-world GC. And C extensions assumed the GIL, so they must opt in via Py_mod_gil, or the GIL comes back.

Q · Failure — After switching a threaded service to 3.14t, counters drift and one endpoint got slower instead of faster. Diagnose. Drift: unsynchronised read-modify-writes that the GIL used to hide now interleave for real (see Break it); fix with locks or single-writer queues. Slower: either a C extension without free-threading support re-enabled the GIL (check sys._is_gil_enabled() at startup and the import warning), or threads now contend on one shared object, like a global list, dict or cache (one list for four threads was several times slower than a list each). Fix: per-thread or sharded state.

Q · Design — Would you move a CPU-heavy Python inference service from processes to free-threaded threads? How? The upside is one shared model instead of one copy per process, plus no pickling. Gate it on evidence: every compiled dependency must declare support (check py-free-threading), the model must be read-only during inference, and shared mutable state must be audited. Run a canary on 3.14t, assert sys._is_gil_enabled() is False at startup, load-test throughput, p99 and RSS against the process-based baseline, and keep processes as the fallback. Watch the GIL-enabled flag and lock contention first.

⚖️ Compare

GIL build Free-threaded build Processes Sub-interpreters
Parallel Python no yes yes yes (one GIL each)
Shared heap yes yes no no
Races on shared state hidden often visible none by default none by default
Main cost no CPU parallelism ~1–8% speed, ~15–20% memory, extension support pickling, RAM per process isolation, 3.14 APIs

🚫 Pitfalls

  • ❌ "No GIL means my threaded code just gets faster"
    ✅ Only if every extension supports it and threads don't contend.
    ↳ Why: one unported extension re-enables the GIL for the whole process; shared objects serialise on their locks.
    ↳ Check: log sys._is_gil_enabled() at startup.
  • 🪞 "My code was thread-safe because it never broke"
    ✅ The GIL was hiding races.
    ↳ Proof: += across four threads went from 800,000 to ~225,000 of 800,000 (see Break it).
  • ❌ "Built-in containers are now fully thread-safe"
    ✅ Single operations are protected; sequences and iteration aren't.
    ↳ Symptom: iterating while another thread mutates can show duplicated or missing items.
  • 🔀 Not the same as sub-interpreters
    ↳ Difference: free-threading shares one heap with no GIL; sub-interpreters keep isolated heaps, one GIL each (#39).
    ↳ So: free-threading needs locking; sub-interpreters need message passing.
  • ⚠️ Don't size thread pools by CPU count without checking the GIL is off.
    ↳ Why: if an extension re-enabled it, the extra threads just take turns.
    ↳ Instead: size from sys._is_gil_enabled() at startup.
  • ⚠️ Don't share one mutable hot object across many threads.
    ↳ Why: its per-object lock becomes a serialisation point (one shared list was several times slower).
    ↳ Instead: per-thread or sharded state, merged later.
  • 🔖 Version: experimental in 3.13t, officially supported in 3.14t (PEP 779), still not the default build.
    ↳ Note: timings are 3.14.6 vs 3.14.6t on a 10-core Mac; overhead figures are the HOWTO's pyperformance averages.

🔗 Links

⬆️ Before: the-gil — what's being removed · synchronization-hazards — the races that now show ⬇️ Next: sub-interpreters — the isolated alternative · interpreter-level-speedups — free-threading and the JIT in practice

notes.title: Sub-Interpreters
notes.html:
📚 References

📘 concurrent.interpreters (3.14) · 📜 PEP 684: A per-interpreter GIL

⚡ TL;DR

Sub-interpreters: many isolated interpreters, one GIL each, one process. Parallel like processes, lighter than processes, and like processes they share nothing.

🎯 Recall

Prompt Answer
What's a sub-interpreter? An isolated interpreter in the same process: own modules, globals and (3.12+) own GIL.
Which versions? Per-interpreter GIL 3.12 (C API); Python API and InterpreterPoolExecutor 3.14.
vs processes / free-threading? Isolated and parallel like processes, in one process; nothing shared, unlike free-threading.

💡 The idea

One interpreter means one GIL, and processes cost startup and pickling. A sub-interpreter is a second isolated interpreter inside the same process; since 3.12 (PEP 684) each has its own GIL, and 3.14 added concurrent.interpreters and InterpreterPoolExecutor. On the standard 3.14.6 build, four CPU-bound jobs took ~0.25 s on an interpreter pool vs ~0.9–1.0 s sequentially. Data is copied or queued between them, and C extensions must support multiple interpreters.

💻 Code

from concurrent.futures import InterpreterPoolExecutor   # 3.14+
from cpu_mod import cpu        # must be importable: each interpreter re-imports it

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with InterpreterPoolExecutor(4) as ex:               # 4 interpreters, 4 GILs, 1 process
        print(list(ex.map(cpu, [10_000_000] * 4)))       # parallel on a GIL build
